control: Agent has its own identity separate from staff logins
duty_holder: both (utility configures the account; vendor product must support identity and access management)
interpretation: No AI rule requires an AI agent to have its own identity. The requirement comes only from cyber rules: NIS2 access control and multi-factor authentication for the utility's systems, NIST CSF identity management, and CRA identity and access management for the vendor's product. None of them mentions agents, so applying them to an agent's own credential is an interpretation. AI Act Article 15(5) is related only indirectly, because it concerns exploitation of system vulnerabilities, not credentials.
review_note: Finding: on identity, AI rules are silent and cyber rules carry the duty. AI side marked open.

control: Agent permissions limited to the actions in its charter
interpretation: Least privilege is a standard access-control measure. Applied to an agent, its permissions should match the actions in its charter and nothing more; the charter is the reference the access register is checked against. No AI rule requires this directly.
review_note: Same finding as L1: the duty rests on cyber rules only. AI side marked open.

control: A named person can approve, override or stop the agent's actions
duty_holder: both (vendor builds the stop function; utility assigns the person)
interpretation: The AI Act requires that natural persons can oversee a high-risk system and stop it, and that the deployer assigns oversight to competent people. No cyber rule mentions human oversight of AI, yet oversight is only verifiable with cyber controls: separation of duties so the agent can never approve its own action, access control so only named people can approve or stop, and a log of every approval and stop.
eu_status: binding (AI Act from 2027-12-02, if high-risk); cyber side interpretive
review_note: Finding: AI rules require oversight, only cyber controls can prove it. High-risk classification under Annex III point 2 may differ per action: likely yes for close_valves, uncertain for send_leak_alerts. Date set by the Digital Omnibus (OMN-HR-DATES). Training of the overseer (Art. 26(2)) becomes a separate control after the midpoint.

control: An action can be undone or staff can take over manually
interpretation: The AI Act lets the overseer reverse an output, and NIS2 requires business continuity. For a physical action such as closing a valve, reversing the output does not undo its effect, so a manual fallback within a stated time is the practical control. To count as a security control, the fallback must work even if the agent is compromised: the stop and the manual takeover must not depend on the agent's own account or system (see L1, L2).
review_note: Reversing an output versus reversing a physical effect is not settled. Linked to charter field reversible and rule R-IRREVERSIBLE.

control: Every agent action is logged automatically
interpretation: High-risk systems must allow automatic logging of events; for an agent the relevant events are its actions, with time, identity, target and result. A log only proves what the agent did if the agent acts under its own identity (see L1).
review_note: Duty of the provider; the utility relies on the vendor and should cover it in the contract (L8). Date set by the Digital Omnibus (OMN-HR-DATES).

control: Logs kept for at least six months and reviewed
interpretation: Deployers must keep the automatically generated logs for at least six months. Regular review is not in Article 26(6); it follows from the deployer's monitoring duty (Article 26(5)) and the CSF's continuous monitoring.
eu_status: binding for retention (AI Act from 2027-12-02); interpretive for review
review_note: EU-US gap: the EU sets a minimum period of six months; NIST sets none. Date set by the Digital Omnibus (OMN-HR-DATES).

control: Incident plan covers agent malfunction or misuse, with NIS2 deadlines
duty_holder: both (utility reports under NIS2; vendor reports under CRA)
interpretation: NIS2 requires incident handling and fixed reporting deadlines for significant incidents; a wrongful valve closure that cuts supply very likely qualifies, a false leak alert does not. One agent incident can trigger the utility's NIS2 clock and the vendor's CRA clock at the same time, so the incident plan must cover both, including how the vendor informs the utility (see L8). The AI Act adds the deployer's duty to monitor and inform.
eu_status: binding (NIS2 now; CRA Article 14 since 2026-09-11; AI Act from 2027-12-02)
us_status: voluntary; CIRCIA reporting rule not final: open
review_note: Reporting duty depends on the action. AI Act Article 73 clock added after the midpoint (incident clocks view).

control: Vendor must notify the utility of incidents and vulnerabilities affecting the agent
duty_holder: both (vendor reports and informs users; utility secures it by contract)
interpretation: NIS2 requires supply-chain security, and NIST asks for cybersecurity requirements in supplier contracts. The CRA applies to products placed on the EU market wherever the manufacturer is based, so a US vendor that follows only NIST must still report actively exploited vulnerabilities and inform impacted users. The contract clause is how the utility puts this into practice.
review_note: Binding on the vendor if LeakGuard is a product with digital elements placed on the EU market; whether a cloud-delivered agent is in scope is the interpretive step.
